aiSummary: Choctawhatchee Bay is fishing well heading into this Friday, with speckled trout active throughout the system and bull redfish showing in quality numbers — recent reports include a 26-lb, 40-inch bull red out of the Santa Rosa Beach area. Conditions today start calm with light ESE winds and mostly sunny skies, but a 34% storm chance arrives before 4 PM, so plan to be off or near shelter by early afternoon. Hit the water at or just after first light to maximize the falling tide window and beat both the heat and the weather.

bridge.aiNote: The 331 Bridge spans a narrow neck of the bay, creating a current funnel that concentrates baitfish on both tides — pilings hold trout, redfish, sheepshead, and black drum year-round. The lee-side pilings are the prime ambush zone on incoming tides, as fish stack up to intercept passing bait. Keep in mind this is open, exposed water — it's typically the first spot on the bay to become unfishable when wind or chop builds.
bridge.todaysCall: The falling tide running toward low at 12:39 PM will push bait through the bridge funnel all morning — work the downcurrent side of the pilings with live shrimp or a paddle-tail on a jighead for trout and reds. Light ESE winds at 5 mph keep conditions fishable here early, but this exposed spot will be the first to get rough if storms develop ahead of the 4 PM window, so plan to wrap up or relocate by noon. Slightly stained water today actually favors darker or chartreuse soft plastics that give fish a clear target in reduced visibility. The waning crescent moon delivers a moderate tidal push — not a screaming outgo, but enough flow to keep bait moving through the structure.

alaqua.aiNote: Alaqua Bayou offers protected water with a strong year-round redfish population, plus trout and flounder near the mouth. The oyster bars at the creek mouth are the prime focal point, and tree cover keeps interior temperatures a few degrees cooler than the open bay while providing natural shelter from wind and weather. The upper creek transitions toward brackish conditions and can hold largemouth bass alongside smaller redfish.
alaqua.todaysCall: With the falling tide moving water out through the morning, position on or just upcurrent of the oyster bars at the creek mouth — reds and trout will be holding on the edges waiting for bait to wash by. The tree canopy here will be a genuine asset on a high-84°F day, keeping the water a touch cooler and making fish more aggressive through the midday hours. Slightly stained water is typical for this creek system and shouldn't hurt the bite — weedless gold spoons or shrimp under a popping cork both work well in this visibility. If the storm threat materializes before 4 PM, Alaqua's tree cover and protected layout make it one of the better spots to shelter in place or safely call the trip.

basin.aiNote: Basin Bayou sees lighter pressure than nearby Alaqua and LaGrange, which tends to produce less-educated fish willing to bite. The interior grass flats are classic sight-fishing territory for redfish in water under two feet, and pompano occasionally appear at the mouth on moving tides in late spring and early summer. It offers less weather protection than LaGrange when conditions deteriorate.
basin.todaysCall: Start on the interior grass flats at first light for sight-casting to reds — the falling tide will concentrate fish on flat edges and points as water drains off the grass, and low light gives you the best shot before the sun gets high and fish spook. With only 5 mph of ESE wind, wade-fishing or poling a skiff is very manageable here this morning. The bay-wide redfish bite has been solid, and Basin's lower pressure means these fish likely haven't seen many presentations — natural-colored soft plastics or a weedless gold spoon are your best calls in slightly stained water. Be mindful that Basin offers less protection than LaGrange if storms build early; have a exit plan ready well before the pre-4 PM storm window.

lagrange.aiNote: LaGrange Bayou is widely considered the top trout producer among the local bayous, with legendary oyster bars at the mouth and interior grass flats that hold redfish year-round. Deep interior holes also hold black drum and sheepshead. It is the most protected water on this side of the bay, making it the default choice when weather builds.
lagrange.todaysCall: The falling tide running to low at 12:39 PM sets up perfectly for LaGrange's oyster-bar bite — work the edges with live shrimp or a suspending twitch bait as water drains off the bars and fish stack in the adjacent troughs. Bay-wide reports confirm speckled trout are active throughout the system right now, and LaGrange's bars are as good a bet as any for numbers and quality fish this time of year. Slightly stained water is no problem here — a chartreuse or root beer paddle-tail will draw strikes in reduced visibility. Even if storms develop before 4 PM, LaGrange's protected layout gives you options: tuck further inside to the deep holes for drum and sheepshead and wait it out safely.

fourmile.aiNote: Four Mile Creek is a tidal creek running between Shipyard Marina and the bay, with tidal flow that pushes baitfish up the creek on incoming tides and concentrates redfish and trout in the bends and grass edges. The creek mouth is a recognized flounder zone, and the upper section transitions toward brackish water that can hold bass alongside smaller reds. It is short and well-protected, making it one of the safest options on the bay when weather threatens.
fourmile.todaysCall: With the tide falling all morning toward low at 12:39 PM, focus on the bends and grass edges inside the creek where baitfish will be funneled downcurrent and reds and trout will be set up to ambush — this is a particularly productive scenario in this kind of system. The creek mouth is worth a few casts for flounder early before the sun gets high; slightly stained water favors a slow-rolled white or chartreuse grub along the bottom. At 5 mph ESE winds, this creek will be dead calm — ideal for light tackle finesse work. If the storm window arrives ahead of schedule, Four Mile is your best bet to stay fishing safely; it's the most sheltered location on this dashboard.

hogtown.aiNote: Hogtown Bayou is a signature Santa Rosa Beach guide destination and one of the most productive trout flats on Choctawhatchee Bay, with fish consistently stacked on grass in two to four feet of water during summer mornings. Spanish mackerel show at the mouth on moving tides. It sees regular pressure from guides and recreational anglers alike, and it sits further from the 331 Bridge than the other bayous — factor in run time when planning your day.
hogtown.todaysCall: Early morning is the move at Hogtown in August — guides consistently report the best trout action here before 9 AM when fish are active on the grass in two to four feet, and today's mostly sunny forecast means that window will close fast as the sun climbs. Leave the dock well before first light to account for run time and be on the flat at or just after the 6:05 AM sunrise. The falling tide through mid-morning will keep fish active on the grass edges; a popping cork over live shrimp or a topwater early are both proven summer producers. Spanish mackerel may show at the mouth on the tide movement, so keep a rod rigged with a small spoon or Gotcha plug. Factor the pre-4 PM storm window into your return plan — the run back from Hogtown takes time, so don't linger past noon.

mallet.aiNote: Mallet Bayou is a small tributary feeding directly into LaGrange Bayou just south of Freeport. Its direct connection to LaGrange — this dashboard's top trout producer — means the oyster-bar redfish and trout patterns that define LaGrange plausibly extend into this quieter, smaller water. There is less documented fishing history for Mallet Bayou specifically, but its interior, sheltered position makes it a likely calm-water fallback when wind picks up on the open bay.
mallet.todaysCall: Think of Mallet today as a quieter, lower-pressure extension of the LaGrange bite — if the oyster bars at LaGrange's mouth are crowded on a Friday, slip further into Mallet for a similar habitat with far fewer boats. Work any oyster structure or grass edges you find on the falling tide with shrimp or soft plastics in slightly stained water. The light ESE wind and protected interior location mean conditions here will be easy all morning. Given the limited documented history on this spot, treat it as a productive bonus rather than a primary destination — pair it with a LaGrange session for the most efficient use of your day.

mack.aiNote: Mack Bayou sits on the barrier-island (30-A) side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park — a long run from the 331 Bridge that makes it a destination trip rather than a casual stop. It shares the same protected-bayou character as Alaqua and LaGrange, with marsh grass, oyster bars, and a few interior holes, and it sees less pressure simply because of its distance from the main ramps. Hewett Bayou and Buck Bayou sit immediately to the east and are realistically fishable in the same trip.
mack.todaysCall: The long run to Mack is most justified on a calm morning like today — light ESE winds at 5 mph mean a comfortable crossing of the open bay, but keep the pre-4 PM storm window firmly in mind and build your turnaround time accordingly. Once there, work the oyster bars and marsh grass edges on the falling tide for reds and trout; lower pressure here means fish that are generally less wary of presentations. Slightly stained water calls for higher-contrast lures — gold spoons and chartreuse soft plastics are reliable choices. Plan to fish Mack together with Hewett and Buck on the same run to make the distance worthwhile, and be wheels-up for the return trip by late morning to stay ahead of the weather.

hewett.aiNote: Hewett Bayou sits immediately east of Mack Bayou on the barrier-island (30-A) side of the bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, sharing the same oyster bar and marsh-grass habitat as its neighbors. Like Mack, it is a long run from the 331 Bridge and sees light pressure because of that distance. It pairs naturally with Mack and Buck Bayou as part of a single 30-A-side trip.
hewett.todaysCall: Hewett fishes best as part of a combined Mack-Hewett-Buck run — today's calm ESE winds make the crossing manageable, but the pre-4 PM storm window means you need to plan a morning-only trip and commit to leaving by late morning at the latest. Work the mouth's oyster bars first on the falling tide for the best trout and redfish action, then probe the deeper interior holes further in. Light pressure here means fish are typically more willing — a natural-color paddle-tail or live shrimp on a jighead is all you need in slightly stained water. Keep your eye on the western sky for building cells and don't let a good bite hold you past your planned departure time.

buck.aiNote: Buck Bayou is the smallest and least-documented of the three neighboring bayous on the barrier-island (30-A) side of the bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park. Its habitat should mirror its larger neighbors — marsh grass, some oyster structure, and a modest interior — but there is less basis to speak with confidence about its fishing character. It is best treated as a bonus stop on a Mack and Hewett Bayou trip rather than a standalone destination.
buck.todaysCall: If you're already running the 30-A side for Mack and Hewett, Buck is a low-commitment add-on worth a quick exploratory session — today's calm winds make moving between all three very easy. Fish it the same way you would its neighbors: oyster edges and grass lines on the falling tide with soft plastics or shrimp in slightly stained water. Expectations should be modest given the limited track record, but the low pressure and similar habitat mean a genuine chance at reds and trout. Keep Buck as your last stop so you can cut it short if the storm window tightens — it's the easiest one to skip if weather builds faster than forecast.
